categories.label: Linguistic
categories.blurb: Sensitivity to spoken and written language — the machinery of naming, arguing, narrating and persuading.

categories.label: Logical-Mathematical
categories.blurb: Detecting patterns, reasoning deductively, and handling abstraction and quantity.

categories.label: Spatial
categories.blurb: Perceiving, transforming and reconstructing the visual-spatial world in the mind's eye.

categories.label: Musical
categories.blurb: Discriminating pitch, rhythm, timbre and structure — and producing them.

categories.label: Bodily-Kinesthetic
categories.blurb: Using the body with precision, and thinking through physical action and proprioception.

categories.label: Interpersonal
categories.blurb: Reading other people's intentions, motivations and states, and coordinating with them.

categories.label: Intrapersonal
categories.blurb: Accurate self-modelling — knowing your own drives, limits, values and failure modes.

categories.label: Naturalistic
categories.blurb: Recognising, classifying and reasoning about the living world and natural systems.

categories.label: Self-Awareness
categories.blurb: Noticing your own emotional state accurately and in real time, before it drives behaviour.

categories.label: Self-Regulation
categories.blurb: Choosing your response instead of emitting it — impulse control, reappraisal, recovery.

categories.label: Social Awareness
categories.blurb: Empathy and situational read: what others feel, and what the room is actually doing.

categories.label: Relationship Management
categories.blurb: Turning emotional read into outcomes — influence, repair, conflict, and building trust.

categories.label: Abstract Reasoning
categories.blurb: Novel problem solving with no stored answer available — the core of fluid intelligence.

categories.label: Working Memory
categories.blurb: Holding and manipulating information live. The bottleneck almost every other faculty runs through.

categories.label: Processing Speed
categories.blurb: How fast simple operations run — the clock rate underneath fluid reasoning.

categories.label: Crystallized Knowledge
categories.blurb: The accumulated, well-indexed store of facts, models and skills — what fluid ability deposits over time.

nodes.label: Vocabulary Depth
nodes.description: The size and precision of your active lexicon. Depth matters more than breadth: knowing a word's connotation, register and collocations is what lets you deploy it, not merely recognise it.
nodes.why: Words are the handles you grab concepts by — a missing word is usually a missing distinction.

resources.title: The Elements of Eloquence — Mark Forsyth

exercises.label: Add 5 unfamiliar words to your SRS deck with a real sentence each
Review your vocabulary deck to zero
Rewrite a paragraph replacing every vague word with a precise one

nodes.label: Analytical Reading
nodes.description: Reading for structure rather than content: locating the thesis, the load-bearing arguments, and the places the author quietly assumes something. Distinct from reading speed, which mostly trades comprehension for pace.
nodes.why: Most knowledge arrives as text, and unstructured reading leaves almost all of it unretrievable.

resources.title: How to Read a Book — Mortimer Adler & Charles Van Doren

exercises.label: Read a chapter and write its argument in 3 sentences without looking back
Map one article's claims and identify its weakest link

nodes.label: Expository Writing
nodes.description: Turning a tangle of half-formed thought into prose another person can follow. The real work is ordering ideas and cutting everything that does not carry weight.
nodes.why: Writing is the highest-bandwidth debugger for your own thinking — vague prose is almost always vague thought.

resources.title: The Elements of Style — Strunk & White

exercises.label: Write 300 words explaining one idea to a smart stranger
Cut a finished piece by 25% without losing meaning

nodes.label: Rhetoric & Persuasion
nodes.description: Structuring a case for a specific audience: what they already believe, what would actually move them, and which order of claims survives contact with their objections.
nodes.why: A correct idea that cannot be transmitted has almost no effect on the world.

exercises.label: Argue a position you disagree with, in writing, as strongly as you can
Rewrite one argument for a specific hostile audience

nodes.label: Extemporaneous Speaking
nodes.description: Composing coherent, structured speech in real time under social pressure, without a script. Depends heavily on working memory and on tolerance for the pause.
nodes.why: Most high-stakes communication happens live, where you cannot revise.

exercises.label: Record a 2-minute unscripted explanation of a random concept
Speak for 5 minutes on a prompt drawn at random

nodes.label: Second Language
nodes.description: Acquiring a language to functional fluency. Forces explicit attention to grammar, phonology and idiom that native use leaves invisible.
nodes.why: A second language rebuilds your model of how meaning is encoded, and audibly sharpens the first one.

exercises.label: 20 minutes of target-language input (audio or text)
Shadow a native recording for 10 minutes
Hold a 15-minute conversation with a speaker

nodes.label: Deductive Reasoning
nodes.description: Moving from premises to conclusions without leaking. Includes recognising valid forms and, more usefully, spotting the invalid ones that feel persuasive.
nodes.why: It is the substrate every other kind of rigorous argument is built on.

exercises.label: Solve one logic puzzle or grid problem
Find the hidden premise in an argument you encountered today

nodes.label: Proof & Formalism
nodes.description: Constructing an argument that survives an adversarial reader: stating exactly what is assumed, what is claimed, and why each step follows.
nodes.why: Formal proof is the strongest available training for noticing when you have not actually shown what you think you showed.

resources.title: How to Solve It — George Pólya

exercises.label: Prove one small result from scratch, writing every step
Find the flaw in a deliberately broken proof

nodes.label: Probabilistic Thinking
nodes.description: Reasoning under uncertainty with actual numbers: base rates, conditional probability, and updating on evidence rather than on vividness.
nodes.why: Almost every real decision is made under uncertainty, and untrained intuition is reliably miscalibrated.

resources.title: Thinking, Fast and Slow — Daniel Kahneman

exercises.label: Make one dated, numeric prediction with a confidence level
Score last month's predictions and check your calibration

nodes.label: Fermi Estimation
nodes.description: Decomposing an unknown quantity into factors you can each guess within an order of magnitude, then recomposing. Accuracy comes from the decomposition, not from the guesses.
nodes.why: It turns "I have no idea" into a usable number in under a minute, which is often the whole decision.

exercises.label: Estimate one quantity from first principles, then look it up

nodes.label: Algorithmic Thinking
nodes.description: Specifying a procedure precisely enough that a machine — or a stranger — could execute it, including the edge cases you would otherwise have skipped over.
nodes.why: It is the discipline of making vague plans executable, which generalises far beyond code.

resources.title: Algorithms to Live By — Christian & Griffiths

exercises.label: Solve one algorithmic problem end to end
Write an everyday process as unambiguous pseudocode

nodes.label: Systems Thinking
nodes.description: Seeing stocks, flows, feedback loops and delays rather than isolated causes. Explains why interventions that look obvious so often backfire.
nodes.why: Most consequential problems are systems problems, and linear cause-and-effect models get them wrong.

exercises.label: Diagram one situation as a causal loop with feedback
Identify a delay that explains a surprising outcome you saw

nodes.label: Mental Visualization
nodes.description: Generating, holding and inspecting an image in the mind's eye with enough stability to read details off it. Vividness varies enormously between people and is partly trainable.
nodes.why: A stable mental image is a free scratchpad that does not consume verbal working memory.

resources.title: Drawing on the Right Side of the Brain — Betty Edwards

exercises.label: Hold an object in mind for 60s, then draw it from memory
Mentally walk a familiar route naming details at each turn

nodes.label: Mental Rotation
nodes.description: Transforming an imagined object — rotating, reflecting, slicing — and correctly predicting the result. One of the most reliably measurable spatial subskills.
nodes.why: It underwrites geometry, engineering, chemistry and anything where you must see the other side of a shape.

exercises.label: Predict a 3D object's cross-section, then verify it
Solve a cube or 3D puzzle from a scrambled state

nodes.label: Navigation & Mapping
nodes.description: Building an allocentric map of an environment — one that survives you turning around — rather than a chain of turn-by-turn instructions.
nodes.why: Spatial memory is unusually durable, which makes it a powerful scaffold to hang other memories on.

exercises.label: Navigate somewhere without turn-by-turn directions
Sketch a map of a place you visited today from memory

nodes.label: Observational Drawing
nodes.description: Drawing what is actually in front of you rather than the symbol your brain substitutes for it. The difficulty is perceptual, not manual.
nodes.why: It is the fastest way to discover how much of what you "see" is reconstruction rather than observation.

resources.title: Drawing on the Right Side of the Brain — Betty Edwards

exercises.label: Draw one object from life for 15 minutes
Do a blind contour drawing without looking at the page

nodes.label: Diagrammatic Reasoning
nodes.description: Choosing a visual representation that makes the structure of a problem obvious — and recognising when a diagram is smuggling in a false assumption.
nodes.why: The right diagram can collapse a problem that is intractable in words.

resources.title: The Visual Display of Quantitative Information — Edward Tufte

exercises.label: Redraw a problem you are stuck on in a different representation

nodes.label: 3D Modelling & Making
nodes.description: Building physical or digital objects, where a spatial error becomes immediately and unforgivingly visible.
nodes.why: Making closes the loop between imagined structure and real structure faster than any other practice.

exercises.label: Model or build one object from a reference

nodes.label: Pitch Discrimination
nodes.description: Hearing the distance between two notes reliably. Relative pitch is trainable at any age; absolute pitch largely is not, and matters far less than people assume.
nodes.why: It is the perceptual primitive every other musical skill is assembled from.

exercises.label: 10 minutes of interval recognition drills
Identify the intervals in a melody you heard today

nodes.label: Rhythm & Timing
nodes.description: Holding a steady internal pulse, subdividing it, and placing events accurately against it — including deliberately off it.
nodes.why: Precise internal timing is shared machinery with motor control and speech.

resources.title: This Is Your Brain on Music — Daniel Levitin

exercises.label: Clap or play a rhythm against a metronome for 10 minutes
Transcribe the rhythm of a phrase you heard

nodes.label: Harmonic Understanding
nodes.description: Hearing chords as functions inside a key rather than as isolated sounds, and predicting where a progression wants to resolve.
nodes.why: Harmony is the clearest everyday example of perceiving deep structure under a surface pattern.

exercises.label: Work out the chord progression of one song by ear
Identify chord qualities in 10 minutes of drills

nodes.label: Instrumental Practice
nodes.description: Deliberate practice on an instrument: isolating the hardest bar, slowing it below the error threshold, and rebuilding speed from there.
nodes.why: It is one of the few domains where the deliberate-practice loop is unambiguous and the feedback is instant.

exercises.label: 25 minutes of focused practice on your weakest passage
Record yourself and diagnose one specific flaw

nodes.label: Transcription by Ear
nodes.description: Writing down music you can only hear. Forces pitch, rhythm and harmony to operate together at speed, with no visual crutch.
nodes.why: It is the closest thing music has to a full-system integration test of the ear.

exercises.label: Transcribe 8 bars of music by ear

nodes.label: Improvisation
nodes.description: Generating musical ideas in real time inside a set of constraints — composing and executing with no separation between the two.
nodes.why: It trains rapid generation under constraint, the same motion as extemporaneous speech and live problem solving.

exercises.label: Improvise for 10 minutes over a backing track
Improvise using only one constraint (3 notes, one string)

nodes.label: Proprioception
nodes.description: Knowing where your body is without looking. The sense most people never train directly, and the one every other physical skill silently depends on.
nodes.why: You cannot correct a movement you cannot feel, so proprioception sets the ceiling on motor learning.

resources.title: Becoming a Supple Leopard — Kelly Starrett

exercises.label: 5 minutes of balance work with eyes closed
Move through a full joint-by-joint range-of-motion scan

nodes.label: Fine Motor Coordination
nodes.description: Precise, repeatable small movements — the hands doing exactly what was intended, at speed, without conscious supervision.
nodes.why: Fine motor skill is where automaticity becomes visible: the movement frees attention once it stops needing any.

exercises.label: 10 minutes of a fine-motor drill (juggling, typing, instrument)
Practise one skill with your non-dominant hand

nodes.label: Strength & Conditioning
nodes.description: Progressive overload against measurable resistance. The clearest existing model of deliberate practice: quantified load, planned progression, enforced recovery.
nodes.why: Aerobic and resistance training have the best-evidenced effects of any intervention on cognition and mood.

exercises.label: Complete a planned training session
30 minutes of zone-2 aerobic work

nodes.label: Motor Skill Acquisition
nodes.description: Deliberately building a new movement pattern: breaking it into parts, practising below failure speed, and chaining it back together.
nodes.why: The acquisition loop here is identical to the one for cognitive skills, but with far faster feedback.

resources.title: The Inner Game of Tennis — Timothy Gallwey
The Art of Learning — Josh Waitzkin

exercises.label: Drill one movement slowly at zero errors for 15 minutes
Film a movement and compare it against a reference

nodes.label: Breath & Somatic Control
nodes.description: Voluntary control of breathing and muscular tension as a direct lever on arousal — the fastest physical route into the nervous system.
nodes.why: It is the shortest path from a physical action to a change in emotional state, which makes it the workhorse of self-regulation.

resources.title: The Body Keeps the Score — Bessel van der Kolk

exercises.label: 5 minutes of paced breathing with a long exhale
Do a progressive muscle relaxation pass

nodes.label: Manual Craft
nodes.description: Working a physical material — wood, food, clay, textile — where the material pushes back and tells you immediately that your model of it was wrong.
nodes.why: Craft grounds abstract planning in a medium that refuses to accept a hand-wave.

resources.title: Shop Class as Soulcraft — Matthew Crawford

exercises.label: Spend 45 minutes making something physical

nodes.label: Active Listening
nodes.description: Listening to understand rather than to reply: reflecting back what you heard and checking it before responding. Much harder than it sounds, because the reply is already forming.
nodes.why: Almost every interpersonal failure traces back to someone answering a question that was not asked.

exercises.label: In one conversation, reflect back before responding
Ask three follow-up questions before offering an opinion

nodes.label: Perspective Taking
nodes.description: Reconstructing another person's model of the situation — what they know, want and fear — as distinct from feeling what they feel.
nodes.why: It is the cognitive half of empathy, and the half that actually predicts behaviour.

resources.title: Harvard Project Zero — Circle of Viewpoints

exercises.label: Write one disagreement from the other side's point of view
State someone's position so well they would endorse it

nodes.label: Nonverbal Reading
nodes.description: Reading posture, face, prosody and timing as signal — while holding your interpretation loosely, because single cues are famously unreliable.
nodes.why: Most of the emotional content of a conversation never reaches the words.

exercises.label: Watch a conversation on mute and infer the emotional arc
Name one nonverbal shift you noticed today and what preceded it

nodes.label: Collaboration
nodes.description: Producing work with others: dividing labour, surfacing disagreement early, and keeping a shared model of the goal that does not silently drift.
nodes.why: Group output is limited far more by coordination quality than by the ability of any member.

exercises.label: Make one implicit team assumption explicit
Give one piece of specific, actionable feedback

nodes.label: Teaching & Explaining
nodes.description: Building an explanation from the learner's existing model rather than from your own — which requires finding out what that model actually is first.
nodes.why: Teaching is the sharpest possible audit of your own understanding: the gaps surface instantly.

resources.title: Made to Stick — Chip & Dan Heath

exercises.label: Explain something you learned today to another person
Write a Feynman-style explanation with no jargon

nodes.label: Negotiation
nodes.description: Finding the trade that both sides prefer to no deal — which means uncovering interests underneath stated positions.
nodes.why: It forces perspective-taking and self-regulation to operate simultaneously under real stakes.

resources.title: Never Split the Difference — Chris Voss

exercises.label: Identify the underlying interest behind one stated position
Prepare a BATNA before a real conversation

nodes.label: Introspective Accuracy
nodes.description: Reporting your own internal state correctly — which research suggests people are much worse at than they believe, especially about motives.
nodes.why: Every plan you make runs on a model of yourself; if that model is wrong, the plans fail for reasons you cannot see.

resources.title: Thinking, Fast and Slow — Daniel Kahneman

exercises.label: Write 10 minutes of unedited journal, then name the real driver
Predict your own behaviour, then check it a week later

nodes.label: Metacognition
nodes.description: Thinking about your own thinking: knowing which strategy you are using, whether it is working, and when to switch.
nodes.why: It is the control loop over every other skill on this map — the thing that decides where effort goes.

exercises.label: Name the strategy you used on a problem and rate its fit
Run a written retrospective on one project or week

nodes.label: Values Clarification
nodes.description: Working out what you actually optimise for, as revealed by your choices rather than by what you say — and reconciling the two.
nodes.why: Undeclared values still steer every decision; making them explicit is what makes trade-offs negotiable.

resources.title: Man's Search for Meaning — Viktor Frankl

exercises.label: Audit one decision against your stated values
Rank your top five values and force the ties apart

nodes.label: Attention Management
nodes.description: Directing and sustaining attention on one thing, and noticing the exact moment it has wandered — the noticing is the trainable part.
nodes.why: Attention is the scarce resource; every other faculty is throttled by how much of it you can hold on target.

exercises.label: One 50-minute distraction-free deep work block
10 minutes of focused-attention meditation

nodes.label: Growth Orientation
nodes.description: Treating ability as trainable and failure as information. Practically, it shows up as what you do in the first ten seconds after being wrong.
nodes.why: It determines whether difficulty makes you practise more or avoid the domain entirely.

exercises.label: Log one mistake and what it taught you, without self-attack
Deliberately attempt something above your current level

nodes.label: Reflective Solitude
nodes.description: Sustained unstimulated time — no input, no phone — which is when consolidation and the genuinely novel connections tend to happen.
nodes.why: Insight is mostly a background process, and it needs unfilled time to run in.

exercises.label: 30 minutes with no input — walk, sit, or stare

nodes.label: Field Observation
nodes.description: Looking at the living world closely enough to notice what is actually there rather than what you expect — the same discipline as observational drawing, applied outdoors.
nodes.why: Careful observation is the raw input to every classification and every hypothesis.

resources.title: The Laws Guide to Nature Drawing and Journaling — John Muir Laws

exercises.label: Observe one organism for 10 minutes and write what you saw
Keep a dated nature-journal entry with a sketch

nodes.label: Classification & Taxonomy
nodes.description: Sorting things by the features that actually carve nature at its joints, and learning to distrust the superficial resemblances that mislead.
nodes.why: Building a good category system is the general skill behind every ontology, schema and mental model.

exercises.label: Identify 3 species to genus and record what distinguished them
Build a small dichotomous key for a group you know

nodes.label: Ecological Reasoning
nodes.description: Reasoning about interdependence, energy flow and population feedback — systems thinking where the system is alive and the delays are long.
nodes.why: Ecosystems are the most legible large-scale example of feedback, delay and non-obvious second-order effects.

resources.title: The Hidden Life of Trees — Peter Wohlleben

exercises.label: Trace one food web or nutrient cycle in a local habitat

nodes.label: Natural Pattern Recognition
nodes.description: Spotting recurring form in nature — branching, spirals, tessellation, scaling laws — and recognising the same generative rules across unrelated systems.
nodes.why: The same handful of patterns reappear in biology, finance and networks; learning them once pays out everywhere.

exercises.label: Find one natural pattern and name its generating rule

nodes.label: Seasonal & Cyclical Awareness
nodes.description: Tracking slow cycles — weather, migration, light, growth — over months. Training for a timescale most attention never operates on.
nodes.why: It builds patience with long feedback loops, which is exactly what long-horizon skill development requires.

exercises.label: Record one dated phenological observation

nodes.label: Natural Navigation
nodes.description: Orienting by sun, stars, wind, vegetation and terrain rather than by instrument — reading direction off the environment itself.
nodes.why: It fuses spatial reasoning with field observation and works when nothing else does.

exercises.label: Determine north without a compass or phone, then verify

nodes.label: Emotional Granularity
nodes.description: Distinguishing "anxious" from "apprehensive" from "resentful" instead of collapsing everything into good or bad. People with finer emotional vocabulary regulate measurably better.
nodes.why: You cannot act on a feeling you can only describe as "off" — precision in naming is what makes a response selectable.

resources.title: How Emotions Are Made — Lisa Feldman Barrett
Atlas of the Heart — Brené Brown

exercises.label: Name your current emotion with a specific word, three times today
Log the day's emotions and their triggers

nodes.label: Interoception
nodes.description: Reading the body's internal signals — heart rate, gut, jaw, breath — which usually register a state change before conscious awareness does.
nodes.why: The body reports the emotion first, so interoception buys you the seconds in which regulation is still possible.

resources.title: The Body Keeps the Score — Bessel van der Kolk
Greater Good in Action — Body Scan

exercises.label: Do a 5-minute body scan and note three sensations
Catch one physical signal of stress before it escalates

nodes.label: Trigger Mapping
nodes.description: Cataloguing the specific situations that reliably knock you off balance, and the early signature of each — usually a small set that repeats for years.
nodes.why: A known trigger is a planned-for trigger; an unknown one just looks like the world being unfair.

exercises.label: Log one trigger, its early signal, and your response
Review the week's triggers and find the common pattern

nodes.label: Bias Awareness
nodes.description: Catching your own motivated reasoning in flight — noticing when a conclusion arrived suspiciously fast because you wanted it.
nodes.why: Bias is invisible from the inside by construction, so only a trained habit of checking catches it.

resources.title: Thinking, Fast and Slow — Daniel Kahneman

exercises.label: Find one belief you hold partly because it is convenient
Run a pre-mortem on a decision you are about to make

nodes.label: Feedback Seeking
nodes.description: Actively soliciting information about how you land on other people, and receiving it without defending — the second part being the hard one.
nodes.why: Self-perception and how you actually land diverge quietly; outside data is the only correction available.

resources.title: Thanks for the Feedback — Stone & Heen

exercises.label: Ask one person for specific feedback and only ask questions back

nodes.label: Narrative Audit
nodes.description: Examining the story you tell about yourself — the recurring roles and explanations — and testing whether it still fits the evidence.
nodes.why: Self-narrative silently constrains what you attempt, long after the events that formed it stopped being relevant.

exercises.label: Write one recurring self-story and list evidence against it

nodes.label: Impulse Control
nodes.description: Inserting a gap between stimulus and response. The gap does not need to be long — it needs to exist at all.
nodes.why: Nearly every action people regret was available for reconsideration for about two seconds.

exercises.label: Pause 10 seconds before one reactive response
Delay one urge by 20 minutes and note what changed

nodes.label: Cognitive Reappraisal
nodes.description: Changing how you feel by changing how you frame the situation. The best-evidenced regulation strategy, and far more effective than suppression.
nodes.why: Reappraisal alters the emotion itself; suppression only hides it and costs more to maintain.

exercises.label: Reframe one frustrating event in a plausible alternative way
Write the automatic thought and a balanced counter-thought

nodes.label: Distress Tolerance
nodes.description: Staying functional while feeling bad, instead of acting purely to make the feeling stop. Discomfort becomes something you can carry rather than something you must resolve.
nodes.why: Most avoidance is not fear of the task but unwillingness to feel the discomfort of starting it.

resources.title: DBT Skills Training Handouts — Marsha Linehan

exercises.label: Sit with one uncomfortable feeling for 5 minutes without fixing it
Do the task you have been avoiding, badly, for 10 minutes

nodes.label: Recovery & Sleep
nodes.description: Protecting sleep and genuine downtime. Sleep debt degrades emotional regulation and working memory faster than almost any other variable.
nodes.why: Every faculty on this map runs worse on a tired brain, so recovery is the cheapest multiplier available.

exercises.label: Hit your target sleep window
Take a real break with no screen

nodes.label: Habit Design
nodes.description: Engineering the environment and cues so the desired behaviour is the path of least resistance, rather than relying on willpower to win every time.
nodes.why: Willpower is a depleting resource; structure is not, and structure is what makes practice survive bad weeks.

exercises.label: Remove one point of friction from a habit you want
Write one implementation intention: when X, I will Y

nodes.label: Delayed Gratification
nodes.description: Weighting a distant payoff correctly against an immediate one, in the moment when the immediate one is loud and present.
nodes.why: Every skill on this map pays out on a horizon of months, which makes discounting the enemy of all of them.

exercises.label: Choose the long-horizon option in one real trade-off

nodes.label: Empathic Accuracy
nodes.description: Correctly inferring what another person is feeling — and, critically, checking the inference rather than trusting it.
nodes.why: Confident empathy that is wrong does more damage than admitted uncertainty.

exercises.label: Guess someone's feeling, then ask and compare
Name the unmet need behind someone's complaint

nodes.label: Compassion
nodes.description: Empathy plus the motivation to help, deliberately trained. Unlike raw empathic distress, compassion does not burn out under exposure.
nodes.why: Empathy alone exhausts; compassion is the sustainable form and produces better outcomes for both parties.

exercises.label: 10 minutes of loving-kindness practice
Do one unprompted, useful thing for someone

nodes.label: Situational Read
nodes.description: Reading a group rather than an individual: who holds status, what is unsaid, and which norms are actually in force here.
nodes.why: The right thing said into the wrong room lands as the wrong thing.

exercises.label: In one group, note the unspoken rule everyone is following

nodes.label: Cultural Fluency
nodes.description: Recognising that directness, hierarchy, time and disagreement are encoded differently across cultures, and adjusting without condescending.
nodes.why: Most cross-cultural friction is a decoding error, not a disagreement about substance.

exercises.label: Identify one norm you assumed was universal

nodes.label: Listening for Subtext
nodes.description: Hearing the concern underneath the stated question — what the person is really asking about, which is often not the topic.
nodes.why: Answering the literal question while missing the real one is the most common form of unhelpful help.

exercises.label: Identify the real concern behind one surface question

nodes.label: Reading Boundaries
nodes.description: Detecting where someone's limits are — often signalled indirectly — and treating a soft no as a no.
nodes.why: Trust is built far more by respecting an unspoken limit than by any amount of stated goodwill.

resources.title: Set Boundaries, Find Peace — Nedra Glover Tawwab

exercises.label: Notice one indirect no and honour it without pressing

nodes.label: Trust Building
nodes.description: Accumulating reliability over time: doing what you said, at the size you said, repeatedly. Slow to build and fast to lose.
nodes.why: Trust is the bandwidth limit on every relationship — nothing difficult can be said without it.

resources.title: The Speed of Trust — Stephen M. R. Covey

exercises.label: Make one small commitment and keep it exactly
Say one true thing you would normally soften

nodes.label: Conflict Navigation
nodes.description: Staying in a disagreement productively: separating the person from the problem, and the impact from the intent.
nodes.why: Avoided conflict does not disappear, it compounds — and arrives later at a worse moment.

exercises.label: Raise one small issue instead of letting it pass
Separate impact from intent in one disagreement

nodes.label: Rupture & Repair
nodes.description: Acknowledging harm specifically, without a defence attached, and changing the behaviour. Repair reliably matters more than never rupturing.
nodes.why: Relationships are not distinguished by an absence of rupture but by the speed and honesty of repair.

exercises.label: Apologise for one specific thing with no "but"

nodes.label: Ethical Influence
nodes.description: Moving people by making the genuinely better option clearer and easier — the line between influence and manipulation being whether it survives them knowing what you did.
nodes.why: Influence without the ethical constraint destroys the trust that made it possible in the first place.

exercises.label: Persuade by improving the other side's information, not pressure

nodes.label: Mentoring & Sponsorship
nodes.description: Deliberately raising someone else's capability — and spending your own credibility on their behalf when they are not in the room.
nodes.why: Teaching someone to competence is the most rigorous test of whether you understand the skill yourself.

resources.title: The Coaching Habit — Michael Bungay Stanier

exercises.label: Ask a coaching question instead of giving the answer

nodes.label: Relationship Maintenance
nodes.description: Keeping weak ties alive with small, non-transactional contact, long before you need anything from them.
nodes.why: Weak ties are the main channel through which genuinely new information and opportunity arrive.

resources.title: The Strength of Weak Ties — Mark Granovetter

exercises.label: Contact one dormant tie with no ask attached

nodes.label: Pattern Abstraction
nodes.description: Extracting the rule that generates a set of examples, then applying it to a case you have never seen. This is what matrix-reasoning tests are actually measuring.
nodes.why: It is the closest thing to a direct measurement of fluid intelligence, and it underlies all genuine transfer.

exercises.label: Solve 10 matrix or sequence reasoning items
State the general rule behind three specific cases you met

nodes.label: Analogical Mapping
nodes.description: Recognising that two situations share relational structure despite sharing no surface features — and noticing when the analogy breaks.
nodes.why: Analogy is the main mechanism by which knowledge from one domain becomes usable in another.

exercises.label: Map a problem onto a structurally similar one from another field
Take an analogy you use and find exactly where it fails

nodes.label: Hypothesis Generation
nodes.description: Producing several candidate explanations rather than committing to the first plausible one, and designing a test that could distinguish them.
nodes.why: Most reasoning failures are failures of imagination at step one, not errors of logic afterwards.

resources.title: The Structure of Scientific Revolutions — Thomas Kuhn

exercises.label: Generate 3 explanations for something surprising, then a test

nodes.label: Novel Problem Solving
nodes.description: Making progress on a problem for which you have no stored procedure — where the work is finding a foothold, not executing a known method.
nodes.why: It is the load-bearing case: fluid ability is exactly what remains when retrieval has nothing to offer.

resources.title: How to Solve It — George Pólya

exercises.label: Work 30 minutes on a problem with no known method
Solve a problem in a domain you have never studied

nodes.label: Inductive Inference
nodes.description: Generalising from limited data while tracking how much the evidence actually supports — including the discipline of not generalising yet.
nodes.why: Real inference almost always runs on insufficient data, so calibrated induction is the practical skill.

exercises.label: State a generalisation and the evidence that would overturn it

nodes.label: Memory Span
nodes.description: How many independent items you can hold available at once. Raw span is quite fixed; what improves is how much you pack into each slot.
nodes.why: Span sets a hard ceiling on how complex a thought you can assemble without writing it down.

exercises.label: Run a digit or sequence span drill for 10 minutes

nodes.label: Chunking
nodes.description: Recoding several items into one meaningful unit, which is how experts appear to hold far more than they do. Chunking is where crystallized knowledge quietly buys you fluid capacity.
nodes.why: It is the one reliable way to get more out of a fixed working-memory span.

exercises.label: Recode a list into meaningful groups and recall it
Find the chunk structure an expert uses in your field

nodes.label: Updating & Inhibition
nodes.description: Replacing what is held in mind as new information arrives, and suppressing the now-irrelevant old contents — the suppression being the harder half.
nodes.why: Stale contents that fail to clear are a common and invisible source of reasoning error.

exercises.label: Run an n-back or updating task for 10 minutes
Deliberately drop a hypothesis that new evidence killed

nodes.label: Mental Manipulation
nodes.description: Transforming held information rather than merely storing it — mental arithmetic, reordering, running a simulation forward in your head.
nodes.why: Storage without manipulation is memory; the manipulation is where the thinking happens.

resources.title: Secrets of Mental Math — Arthur Benjamin

exercises.label: Do 10 minutes of mental arithmetic with no writing
Play a chess or Go position forward 5 moves in your head

nodes.label: Load Management
nodes.description: Recognising when a task has exceeded your capacity and offloading deliberately — to paper, to a diagram, to a checklist — rather than dropping items silently.
nodes.why: The skill is not holding more but knowing precisely when you no longer can.

exercises.label: Notice one overload moment and externalise the state

nodes.label: Perceptual Speed
nodes.description: How fast you can compare, match and discriminate simple stimuli. Largely constitutional, but measurably degraded by fatigue and sleep debt.
nodes.why: It is the clock rate the rest of cognition runs on, and the first thing poor sleep takes away.

exercises.label: Run a reaction-time or visual-search drill

nodes.label: Automaticity
nodes.description: Practising a sub-skill until it runs without supervision, freeing attention for the level above it. The main mechanism by which experts appear fast.
nodes.why: Every operation you automate hands its working-memory budget back to the harder problem.

exercises.label: Drill one sub-skill to fluency for 15 minutes

nodes.label: Visual Scanning
nodes.description: Sweeping a dense field efficiently for the thing that matters — with a search strategy rather than a random walk.
nodes.why: Most information environments are now dense enough that filtering speed dominates reading speed.

exercises.label: Skim a dense document for one specific fact, timed

nodes.label: Decision Speed
nodes.description: Deciding quickly when the decision is cheap and reversible, and deliberately slowing down when it is neither. The skill is the classification, not the speed.
nodes.why: Treating every decision as high-stakes wastes the budget you need for the ones that are.

resources.title: Thinking, Fast and Slow — Daniel Kahneman
Algorithms to Live By — Christian & Griffiths

exercises.label: Classify a decision as reversible or not, then act accordingly

nodes.label: Input Fluency
nodes.description: Getting thought out of your head and into a medium fast enough that the medium stops being the bottleneck — typing, handwriting, shorthand, tool fluency.
nodes.why: When capture is slow, ideas are lost between having them and recording them.

exercises.label: 10 minutes of typing or capture-speed practice

nodes.label: Retrieval Practice
nodes.description: Recalling from an empty page rather than rereading. The difficulty is the mechanism — effortful retrieval is what strengthens the trace.
nodes.why: It is the single best-evidenced study technique, and it feels worse than the techniques that do not work.

resources.title: Make It Stick — Brown, Roediger & McDaniel

exercises.label: Close the book and write everything you remember
Self-test on last week's material with no notes

nodes.label: Spaced Repetition
nodes.description: Reviewing at expanding intervals timed to just before forgetting. Converts a linear time cost into near-permanent retention.
nodes.why: Without spacing, almost everything you learn is gone within weeks regardless of how well you understood it.

exercises.label: Clear your review queue to zero
Write 5 atomic cards from today's reading

nodes.label: Elaborative Encoding
nodes.description: Connecting new material to what you already know — explaining why it is true, and where it contradicts something else you believe.
nodes.why: Isolated facts have no retrieval routes; elaboration is what builds the paths back to them.

resources.title: Make It Stick — Brown, Roediger & McDaniel

exercises.label: Connect one new fact to three things you already know

nodes.label: Interleaved Practice
nodes.description: Mixing problem types within a session instead of blocking them. Performance during practice drops; retention and transfer rise.
nodes.why: Blocked practice teaches you to execute a method; interleaving teaches you to choose one.

resources.title: Make It Stick — Brown, Roediger & McDaniel

exercises.label: Mix three problem types in one practice session

nodes.label: Method of Loci
nodes.description: Hanging arbitrary information on a vividly imagined route through a familiar place, exploiting how durable spatial memory is.
nodes.why: It converts material your memory ignores into material it is built to hold.

exercises.label: Memorise a 20-item list using a memory palace

nodes.label: Knowledge System
nodes.description: An external store with real linking, so that past thinking is retrievable and can collide productively with new material. An unindexed archive is not a knowledge system.
nodes.why: Memory is lossy and associative; a linked external store is the prosthesis that makes long-term synthesis possible.

resources.title: How to Take Smart Notes — Sönke Ahrens

exercises.label: Write one permanent note in your own words and link it
Link two previously unconnected notes and say why

nodes.label: Mental Model Library
nodes.description: A stocked, cross-disciplinary set of explanatory frames — feedback, incentives, selection, compounding — with a clear sense of where each applies.
nodes.why: A broad model library is what lets you recognise a familiar structure inside an unfamiliar problem.

resources.title: The Model Thinker — Scott E. Page

exercises.label: Apply one named model to a situation from today
Add a model to your library with two worked examples

nodes.label: Knowledge Breadth
nodes.description: Deliberate sampling well outside your specialisation, at enough depth to recognise the structure rather than just the vocabulary.
nodes.why: Breadth is what supplies the source domains that analogical transfer draws on.

exercises.label: Read something substantive far outside your field

nodes.label: Domain Depth
nodes.description: Going deep enough in one field to hold expert-level chunks and to have opinions that survive contact with practitioners.
nodes.why: Depth in one domain is what teaches you what real understanding feels like, so you can recognise its absence elsewhere.

exercises.label: 60 minutes of deliberate practice at your current edge
Produce something a practitioner would critique seriously

nodes.label: Transfer
nodes.description: Actually deploying knowledge in a context unlike the one you learned it in — which happens far less automatically than education assumes.
nodes.why: Knowledge that never transfers is inert, and most of it stays inert unless transfer is practised on purpose.

resources.title: Make It Stick — Brown, Roediger & McDaniel

exercises.label: Use a method from one field on a problem in another

nodes.label: Quantitative Literacy
nodes.description: Reading numbers critically: units, denominators, distributions, and what a statistic is silently leaving out.
nodes.why: Most numeric claims that mislead are technically true, and only the denominator gives them away.

resources.title: How to Lie with Statistics — Darrell Huff

exercises.label: Take one statistic and find its denominator and caveats

nodes.label: Historical Context
nodes.description: Knowing how the present arrangement came about, and therefore which parts of it are contingent rather than inevitable.
nodes.why: Without history, every current arrangement looks like the only one that was ever possible.

resources.title: The Structure of Scientific Revolutions — Thomas Kuhn

exercises.label: Trace the origin of one thing you take for granted

nodes.label: Technical Fluency
nodes.description: Enough command of your tools that they stop competing for attention with the problem you are using them on.
nodes.why: Tool friction is a working-memory tax you pay on every single session until you remove it.

exercises.label: Learn one shortcut or feature that removes recurring friction
